rv.q: It probably won't please literary purists, but it will delight a broad audience, and even those resistant to the unashamedly corny will likely be won over by the breathtaking look and strident performances in this feat of spectacle and seduction.
The book is a masterpiece. The musical is a good attempt. But I liked it, old sport.
In performance this Gatsby turns out to be a sleek, ravishingly designed ocean liner of a show, with enough musical oomph and vocal power to distract you from the hollowness at its heart.
But while it may not fully engage one's emotions, this is a Show with a capital S.

What it lacks (and it lacks a great deal) in meaningful exploration of the themes and ideas that have made this text a classic, it attempts to compensate for with bucketloads of Jazz Age razzle-dazzle.

Let’s not get all lit crit though. The biggest problem here is not so much how the creatives have gone about making a Great Gatsby musical, but rather that it only takes a few minutes to conclude that the very idea of a Great Gatsby musical is inherently flawed.
Where the novel is concise, understated and allusive, this show is big, brash, noisy and oddly one-dimensional.

Instead, we get a screechy clodhopping musical that amps up the Roaring Twenties clichés at the expense of anything Fitzgerald had to say about class, money and the scissoring chasms between appearances and reality.
Fresh from Broadway, this production encapsulates the worst of peacockingly splashy entertainment – the kind whose soul has been suctioned out in the making.
This Great Gatsby is a visually stunning, emotionally resonant, and thoroughly entertaining production.

Jamie Muscato and Frances Mayli McCann nevertheless lend considerable heft to Gatsby and Daisy's doomed recoupling, especially when belting out Jason Howland and Nathan Tysen's colossal Disney-esque power ballads.
The Great Gatsby at the London Coliseum is a triumph of style over substance.
Two and a half hours of tedious hoofing and banal glamour, a band and singer entertaining the freeloaders all the way to hell, a foghorn the metaphor that opens the show.
While it certainly captures the Bacchanalian fizz of jazz-soaked New York, it's less successful at conveying the novel's tortured soul.

When F Scott Fitzgerald’s third novel THE GREAT GATSBY was published in 1925, it was generally considered to be a weaker effort than his earlier works This Side of Paradise and The Beautiful and Damned.

The Great Gatsby isn't a great tuner: it's neither cynical enough to really explore the dark underbelly of the F Scott Fitzgerald story with which it flirts, nor is it distinguished enough to provide the uplift of musical theatre at its best, but it's the epitome of a slick, escapist West End night out.
It's serviceable but there's no wow factor.
Director Marc Bruni's show features a highly talented cast, struggling with substandard material. The show is high on visual opulence, but low on heart and soul.
Scott Fitzgerald's feted novella in the transition to full blown musical.
